transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: OmniHealth x Redwood — Private deployment (VPC/on‑prem) security boundary deep dive
Recorded: 2026-02-10 17:00 UTC
Duration: 52 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Colin O'Donnell, Simran Kaur, Ethan Park, Fatima Noor
OmniHealth: Maya Hernandez, Raj Patel, Elena Smirnova, Tom Briggs

Summary (auto-generated)
- Reviewed Redwood Private deployment boundary: control plane vs data plane responsibilities in customer VPC / on-prem.
- Discussed encryption (in-transit, at-rest), customer-managed keys via KMS, and HSM integration patterns.
- Walked through logging and audit logs (what events exist today, export options, and retention boundaries).
- Identified open items: exact SIEM integration method, network egress restrictions, and incident notification expectations.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Private deployment architecture + shared responsibility
2) Network model (PrivateLink, ingress/egress, admin access)
3) KMS / HSM and key custody
4) Audit logging and operational logs
5) Retention + deletion semantics
6) Support model, patching, and incident response boundaries

Action items (auto-generated)
- Colin: send boundary diagram + responsibilities matrix for VPC and on-prem options
- Ethan: send SSO/RBAC + break-glass admin note and auditability guidance
- Simran: send audit log sample events and export options, plus current limitations
- OmniHealth (Raj/Elena): confirm preferred key management + whether HSM is mandatory

Transcript

[00:00] Colin O'Donnell: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Colin from Redwood. The goal today, as I understand it, is to go deeper on the Private deployment model—VPC and potentially on-prem—and specifically the security boundary. We can also cover audit logs, SIEM export, and KMS or HSM integration.

[00:18] Maya Hernandez: Yep. That’s exactly it. We got the high-level answers in the FAQ, but our security team wants the “what runs where” detail.

[00:26] Raj Patel: And what you can see versus what we can see. Also, key ownership. We’re healthcare, so we’re going to be conservative.

[00:34] Simran Kaur: Makes sense. I’m Simran, solutions architecture. I’ll probably share screen later if that’s ok, but we can keep it verbal.

[00:41] Ethan Park: Ethan here. I cover authn/authz, SSO, RBAC, auditability in the control plane.

[00:46] Fatima Noor: Hi, Fatima. I’m here mostly for regulated workload questions and how we typically document boundaries for procurement.

[00:53] Colin O'Donnell: Great. So first, quick framing: when we say Redwood Private, there are two common shapes.
One is: Redwood control plane is managed by Redwood (hosted by us), and the data plane—model serving cluster—runs in your VPC. The other is a “private control plane” variant where more of the control plane is isolated, and then there’s on‑prem / air‑gapped packaging which is… similar concepts, different operational story.

[01:18] Elena Smirnova: For us it’s VPC first. On-prem is like a later phase, but it will come up.

[01:25] Colin O'Donnell: Perfect. For VPC Private: the inference runtime and traffic handling sits in your VPC. Your apps talk to an endpoint that is private to your network—usually via internal load balancer. The control plane is what manages deployments, configs, upgrades, observability, and policy—depending on the exact SKU, that could be reachable via a private connectivity option.

[01:47] Raj Patel: When you say “control plane,” are you storing prompts? Like request content?

[01:53] Colin O'Donnell: Good question. In the Private model, we design it so request payloads and generated outputs stay in your environment in the data plane. Control plane handles metadata—like which model version is deployed, settings, and certain operational events. But not the raw prompts by default.

[02:12] Maya Hernandez: “By default” is the phrase that makes legal nervous.

[02:17] Colin O'Donnell: Totally fair. Let me be precise: in the VPC data plane, the inference service processes requests in your network. Any logging of request/response content is something you can disable, or it is not collected by our managed services in that plane. What we do collect for operating the system are operational metrics and audit events. We can provide a written boundary statement for what telemetry leaves the VPC in the standard configuration.

[02:44] Tom Briggs: So you have like a standard architecture doc we can attach to our risk assessment?

[02:48] Fatima Noor: Yes. We have a “shared responsibility” matrix and a boundary diagram that is intended for exactly that. We’ll send it after. (And we can align it to VPC vs on‑prem.)

[03:00] Simran Kaur: And if you do want content logging, like prompts for debug, that’s an explicit opt-in and we’d typically recommend doing it into your own logging stack in VPC.

[03:12] Raj Patel: Okay. Now network. We prefer no public ingress, obviously. And limited egress.

[03:18] Elena Smirnova: Ideally zero egress except to a few allowlisted endpoints.

[03:23] Colin O'Donnell: Yep. Common. The inference endpoint stays internal. For control plane connectivity, we can do a private link / private endpoint model depending on cloud—AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link, similar patterns. For egress, we need to talk through what things require outbound access: container images, security updates, and optionally sending metrics to Redwood.

[03:44] Elena Smirnova: For container images, can we mirror them into our registry?

[03:48] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, we have customers who do that. It becomes more like an “on-prem style” ops model but still in VPC: you control the artifact store, we provide signed images and manifests. Then upgrades are a coordinated process.

[04:04] Maya Hernandez: Who patches the nodes? Like the underlying Kubernetes worker nodes, OS, etc.

[04:10] Colin O'Donnell: That’s where the boundary matters. In the “managed data plane in your VPC” model, we typically define: you own the cloud account/VPC, we run the serving stack within it, but node patching responsibility depends on whether we provision the cluster (e.g., EKS with managed node groups) and what access you grant. Practically, we usually set it up so Redwood can apply platform updates, but it’s governed, audited, and can be scheduled.

[04:35] Raj Patel: I need the details: do you have persistent admin access into our VPC?

[04:39] Simran Kaur: Not “persistent” in the sense of some always-on backdoor. Access is typically via a controlled mechanism (like a dedicated IAM role with time-bound sessions, or your chosen approval workflow). We can also do a model where access is only enabled during a support window.

[04:56] Ethan Park: And we can make sure those access events are auditable—both in your IAM logs (CloudTrail) and in Redwood’s own admin audit logs, depending on the configuration.

[05:08] Raj Patel: That’s good. We require break-glass with ticket reference. Ideally, no access without it.

[05:14] Colin O'Donnell: We’ve done that. We can align to your process. It does mean some incidents take longer if access must be granted manually, but that’s a trade.

[05:26] Maya Hernandez: Okay, key management. We want customer-managed keys. Possibly HSM, not sure. We currently use AWS KMS with CloudHSM for a few systems.

[05:38] Colin O'Donnell: Right. So for encryption: in transit is TLS, internal service-to-service TLS where applicable. At rest: there are a few buckets of data.
- Model weights / artifacts
- KV cache and runtime memory (ephemeral)
- Any persisted logs, metrics, or config state

In VPC Private, we can store persisted components (like logs, configs, maybe a small metadata DB) in your account and use your KMS keys for encryption at rest.

[06:09] Raj Patel: And the model weights themselves, are they encrypted with our key? Or your key?

[06:14] Simran Kaur: If weights are stored in your S3 (or equivalent), they’re encrypted with your KMS key. If they’re pulled from Redwood-managed storage, then that’s a different pattern. For the strict VPC model, we recommend you host the weights in your account so you control encryption and access. Some customers also require that for vendor risk.

[06:35] Elena Smirnova: What about the keys used for application data, like request payload if it touches disk?

[06:41] Colin O'Donnell: In a standard deployment, request payload shouldn’t be written to disk. If you enable request logging, it’s your choice and then it would land in your logging destination, encrypted under your policies.

[06:54] Raj Patel: HSM: can Redwood integrate with CloudHSM? Or like external HSM?

[07:00] Colin O'Donnell: For cloud, the typical integration is: you use KMS, KMS is backed by CloudHSM if you configure it. Redwood doesn’t talk to HSM directly; we talk to KMS APIs to encrypt/decrypt data keys or to use envelope encryption.

[07:16] Raj Patel: So Redwood never gets plaintext of the master key.

[07:18] Colin O'Donnell: Correct. We never receive your CMK material. We call KMS for cryptographic operations, under IAM policies you control.

[07:27] Tom Briggs: We’ll need that stated pretty explicitly. Also rotation.

[07:31] Fatima Noor: We can provide language: “Customer-managed keys in customer account; Redwood does not have access to key material; key rotation is customer-controlled” etc. But we’ll be careful: what we can guarantee depends on the exact architecture we deploy.

[07:49] Maya Hernandez: Okay, logging. We need two things: audit logs for who did what, and operational logs for troubleshooting. We also need to export to Splunk.

[08:00] Simran Kaur: Great. There’s kind of three layers:
1) Redwood Console / Control plane audit events (e.g., user created API key, changed model routing policy, created deployment)
2) Data plane platform logs (like pods restarting, node health) which in your VPC can be shipped to CloudWatch / your log sink
3) Inference request metrics (latency, tokens) and optionally request-level logs

[08:25] Raj Patel: The big question: do you log prompts or outputs.

[08:29] Simran Kaur: Not by default in Private. We log metadata like request ID, timestamp, model, token counts, latency buckets. If you enable additional logging, it’s configurable, and you can direct it to your SIEM.

[08:44] Elena Smirnova: How do we export audit logs? Is it like an API? Or do we scrape something.

[08:50] Ethan Park: For the control plane audit logs: there’s an export mechanism. In Hosted it’s via the console/API and optionally webhooks. In Private, depending on the control plane placement, we can either: (a) push audit events into your account (like an S3 bucket / event bus), or (b) allow your SIEM to pull from an endpoint. I need to confirm which option you’re evaluating, but both patterns are used.

[09:15] Raj Patel: We prefer push into our account. Pull is always a pain with firewall.

[09:19] Ethan Park: That’s generally the recommendation.

[09:22] Colin O'Donnell: Also, on the “what’s logged today” piece, we can share the current event catalog. There are categories like: auth events, config changes, deployment actions, access grants. We’ll also call out gaps—we don’t want to overpromise.

[09:39] Raj Patel: Are admin actions by Redwood staff logged as well?

[09:43] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, and we can talk about two types:
- Actions taken in the control plane by Redwood operators (these are audit logged)
- Actions taken inside your cloud account using IAM roles (those are visible to you via CloudTrail). We can correlate via ticket IDs where possible.

[10:04] Maya Hernandez: What about the on-prem scenario? If we do air gapped, do we lose all audit logs?

[10:11] Simran Kaur: You don’t lose them, but the storage and export are entirely within your environment. Like, we can ship logs to your ELK/Splunk. But you wouldn’t have Redwood-hosted log retention, because it’s disconnected.

[10:24] Tom Briggs: So in on-prem, we are responsible for retention policies.

[10:27] Colin O'Donnell: Correct. On-prem is more “you run it,” Redwood supports it. We can still provide updates and guidance, but you operate the infra.

[10:39] Raj Patel: Can we talk retention? Specifically for audit logs, how long do you keep them.

[10:44] Ethan Park: In Hosted there are retention defaults and some configurable retention depending on tier. For Private, if logs are stored in your account, you set retention. If any control plane audit logs are stored in Redwood systems, we can provide the retention statement and deletion process, but for Private the goal is to keep the sensitive event data in your environment.

[11:09] Maya Hernandez: If there is a control plane hosted by you, what customer data exists there.

[11:14] Colin O'Donnell: Typically: org metadata, user identities, config, and audit events. Not inference content. But we will document it. If your requirement is “no data leaves,” then you’re really in private control plane / on-prem territory.

[11:33] Elena Smirnova: We might be okay with org metadata leaving, but not request content.

[11:37] Raj Patel: Same. But we need to ensure debug logs don’t accidentally include payload.

[11:44] Simran Kaur: Good catch. We’ve done hardening for that: we avoid logging request bodies. Still, we can show you config flags to disable verbose logging and we can do a review with your team.

[12:01] Raj Patel: Is there any support tooling that “screenshares” our environment or captures request traffic.

[12:06] Colin O'Donnell: No passive capture. Support is generally through logs you provide and metrics. If you authorize access for a support window, we may inspect system state, but not copy inference traffic.

[12:21] Maya Hernandez: Let’s talk about auth. We need SSO, ideally SAML, and RBAC: different teams can view metrics, but only a few can deploy.

[12:31] Ethan Park: Yep. Redwood supports SSO via SAML for the console, and RBAC roles. In Private, same control plane capabilities apply. We also support SCIM in some setups—depending on tier—so you can automate provisioning/deprovisioning.

[12:51] Raj Patel: Can we enforce MFA.

[12:53] Ethan Park: With SSO, MFA is enforced by your IdP. For local accounts (if any are allowed), we can restrict or disable local auth, again depending on the enterprise setup.

[13:09] Tom Briggs: Audit log includes login events?

[13:12] Ethan Park: Yes—SSO logins, failed logins, token/API key creation, role changes, policy changes. I’ll send a list of event types.

[13:24] Elena Smirnova: Switching back: inference data plane logs. If we run in EKS, can we ship to CloudWatch, then to Splunk.

[13:30] Simran Kaur: Exactly. Or you can run fluentbit/otel collector and send direct to Splunk HEC. We can provide a recommended deployment.

[13:41] Raj Patel: We require log integrity. Do you have signing.

[13:45] Colin O'Donnell: For control plane audit logs, we can provide controls description (immutability, restricted access). For data plane logs in your environment, you can implement WORM storage or immutability in S3/Object Lock and sign at ingestion if needed.

[14:04] Maya Hernandez: What about vulnerability management? Who scans images.

[14:08] Colin O'Donnell: Redwood scans our images as part of our SDLC. In Private, you can also scan them in your pipeline. Patching cadence is something we agree on. Criticals get prioritized.

[14:22] Raj Patel: We’ll ask for remediation SLA.

[14:24] Fatima Noor: We can share our vulnerability management summary. For contract SLAs, that’s usually in enterprise terms, but we can provide the standard posture doc.

[14:37] Tom Briggs: SOC 2 scope question. If data plane runs in our VPC, does your SOC 2 cover it.

[14:44] Colin O'Donnell: SOC 2 covers Redwood’s systems and processes. For components in your VPC that we operate, the boundary can be nuanced—there’s still a shared responsibility. We generally provide a statement explaining which controls are ours vs yours. We can also share a bridge letter / description under NDA.

[15:08] Raj Patel: Understood. I just need to say “vendor has SOC 2,” and then show our compensating controls for the rest.

[15:15] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly.

[15:18] Simran Kaur: Also, practically, your risk team will want: architecture diagram, access model, logging/audit, encryption/key management, incident response contacts.

[15:28] Maya Hernandez: Incident response: if there’s an incident in the data plane, who notifies whom.

[15:33] Colin O'Donnell: In VPC model, if it’s your cloud incident (like AWS region issue), you’ll see it. If it’s a Redwood software vulnerability or issue affecting the serving stack, we coordinate. Notification timelines are contract-dependent, so we’ll keep wording careful. But we do have a process and a security contact.

[15:55] Raj Patel: I’m going to push: do you commit to 24 hours.

[15:58] Colin O'Donnell: We can’t promise a blanket 24 hours for all incident types in a meeting like this. The contract language defines “Security Incident” and notification timing. Operationally, we do move quickly, but we will point you to the approved incident notification statement.

[16:17] Tom Briggs: Fine. We’ll look at the template.

[16:20] Elena Smirnova: Operational responsibilities. If the cluster is down at 2 AM, who is on call.

[16:26] Colin O'Donnell: We can do 24/7 support in enterprise tiers. For Private, it’s usually a joint on-call model: you’re responsible for cloud primitives (VPC routing, IAM, quotas) and we’re responsible for Redwood components (serving runtime, control plane agents). But again, exact split depends on whether we manage the cluster or you do.

[16:51] Maya Hernandez: We prefer you to manage the Redwood stack, but we will manage the AWS account. That’s likely.

[16:57] Colin O'Donnell: That’s the most common.

[17:00] Raj Patel: Let’s do a concrete flow. Request comes from our app to your endpoint. Where does it traverse.

[17:07] Simran Kaur: Sure. In VPC: your app → internal LB → inference gateway service → model server pods on GPU nodes. Response goes back same path. No hop to Redwood network. The only “outbound” would be metrics or update checks if enabled.

[17:28] Elena Smirnova: For metrics, can we keep them fully local.

[17:31] Simran Kaur: Yes. We can deploy Prometheus/Grafana in VPC and keep telemetry local. Redwood Console can optionally read summary metrics depending on connectivity. But if your requirement is “no telemetry out,” we can do it.

[17:49] Raj Patel: That will make your support harder though.

[17:52] Colin O'Donnell: It can, but we can work with logs you export to us during a support case, or we do a controlled access session. This is a typical tradeoff.

[18:05] Tom Briggs: Data deletion. If prompts never leave, then deletion is basically our responsibility.

[18:10] Colin O'Donnell: Correct. If you log prompts, you manage deletion. For Redwood metadata (like org records), we have account deletion procedures.

[18:24] Maya Hernandez: Okay. How about model updates. If we pin a version, can you update without us.

[18:30] Colin O'Donnell: In Private we generally encourage version pinning and change windows. We can propose updates, but you control the rollout. Some customers allow auto patching for criticals.

[18:45] Raj Patel: Are model weights coming from you or us.

[18:48] Simran Kaur: For strict setups, you host the weights. We provide the model package and checksum/signature. If you want Redwood to host, that’s feasible but then you need egress and you accept that dependency.

[19:07] Elena Smirnova: Prefer we host.

[19:09] Simran Kaur: Cool.

[19:11] Raj Patel: Back to audit logs. Can we get sample events now.

[19:15] Ethan Park: I don’t have them in front of me in this call, but example would be like:
- user.login.sso.success
- api_key.created
- role.binding.updated
- deployment.created
- routing_policy.updated
- admin_access.granted
Each includes timestamp, actor, target resource, and request ID. We’ll share real schemas after the call.

[19:45] Raj Patel: Are those JSON.

[19:47] Ethan Park: Yes, JSON.

[19:50] Maya Hernandez: SIEM export. We use Splunk Cloud. HEC is easiest.

[19:55] Simran Kaur: We can run an OTel collector or fluentbit in the data plane and forward to Splunk HEC. For control plane audit logs, we can push to S3 and you can have Splunk ingest from there, or push to EventBridge and use a forwarder.

[20:18] Elena Smirnova: Great.

[20:20] Raj Patel: Access again. Redwood staff: are they background checked.

[20:24] Fatima Noor: We can share our compliance posture documentation; employee screening and security training are covered in the program summary. Specifics we can confirm with GRC.

[20:39] Tom Briggs: Okay.

[20:41] Colin O'Donnell: I want to make sure we’re answering the core: security boundary and responsibilities. Let me attempt a quick matrix verbally, and then we’ll send the formal doc.
- OmniHealth: VPC/network controls, IAM in your cloud, base infra approvals, log retention in your account, incident response for cloud-side events, and policy approvals.
- Redwood: inference software stack, configuration guidance, security patches for Redwood components, and support.
- Shared: monitoring, change management windows, and access approval workflow.

[21:19] Maya Hernandez: That’s good. But for on-prem, it shifts.

[21:23] Colin O'Donnell: On-prem: you own and operate the infra fully. Redwood provides the software, updates, and support. Some customers do it in disconnected mode.

[21:37] Raj Patel: Does on-prem support HSM like Thales.

[21:41] Colin O'Donnell: We’ve seen integrations where your storage layer is encrypted with your HSM-backed keys, but Redwood doesn’t directly integrate with a specific vendor in the runtime. Usually it’s through the OS/disk encryption or a key service in your environment.

[22:00] Raj Patel: Okay, so KMS is cloud path; on-prem is more custom.

[22:05] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly.

[22:07] Elena Smirnova: Another question: do you require outbound DNS to your domain.

[22:12] Simran Kaur: Only if you’re connecting to a Redwood-hosted control plane. If you’re using private endpoints, it can still be DNS resolution, but within private hosted zones. For updates, again depends if you mirror artifacts.

[22:30] Maya Hernandez: What about certificate management. Do we use our certs.

[22:34] Colin O'Donnell: For the internal LB endpoint, yes, you can use your certificates. For internal mTLS, we can integrate with your PKI depending on setup, or use a managed CA within your environment.

[22:52] Raj Patel: Do you support FIPS.

[22:55] Colin O'Donnell: In certain environments we can run with FIPS-enabled crypto libraries and OS images. We should treat this as a requirement and validate in the architecture workshop. It impacts base images and sometimes performance.

[23:13] Tom Briggs: We’ll note it as “nice-to-have” for now, but might become hard requirement.

[23:18] Colin O'Donnell: Got it.

[23:20] (cross talk)

[23:22] Simran Kaur: One more logging nuance: there’s “audit logs” and there’s “inference observability.” Inference observability usually includes token counts, latency percentiles, model IDs. That is safe. Any “prompt capture” is a separate flag.

[23:40] Raj Patel: I want to see the config options. Because sometimes vendors say it’s separate, but it’s actually always on.

[23:47] Simran Kaur: Totally. We can show you the helm values / config in the workshop.

[23:54] Maya Hernandez: Okay. How do you handle secrets. Like API keys for pulling weights, Splunk HEC token, etc.

[24:01] Colin O'Donnell: We integrate with secret stores in your environment—Kubernetes secrets, external secrets operator, AWS Secrets Manager, Vault. Recommended is external secrets with your secrets manager.

[24:18] Elena Smirnova: We use AWS Secrets Manager.

[24:20] Colin O'Donnell: Great.

[24:23] Raj Patel: Do you have a list of ports/protocols required.

[24:26] Simran Kaur: Yes, we have a network requirements doc: inbound to the inference endpoint, east-west within cluster, optional outbound to artifact store / update endpoints / control plane. We’ll include it.

[24:42] Tom Briggs: And a subprocessor list. If control plane is hosted by Redwood, we need to know cloud vendors.

[24:48] Fatima Noor: We can share the subprocessor list and how it changes depending on deployment mode. In VPC-only model, subprocessors are limited because the data plane is yours.

[25:03] Raj Patel: Great.

[25:05] Colin O'Donnell: Anything else we haven’t covered: KMS/HSM, logging, boundary.

[25:10] Maya Hernandez: I want to make sure we can meet our internal “no vendor operator without approval” rule.

[25:16] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. We’ll implement time-bound access with your approval. It may require building an operational runbook: how to grant, how to revoke, what happens during incident.

[25:31] Elena Smirnova: We can do that.

[25:33] Raj Patel: And we need to ensure the audit logs show it.

[25:37] Ethan Park: Yep. We’ll include both the Redwood audit trail and your cloud audit trail guidance.

[25:45] Colin O'Donnell: Cool. Maybe we pivot to next steps. Here’s what I captured.

[25:51] Colin O'Donnell: One, we’ll send the boundary diagram and shared responsibility matrix for VPC Private and an on‑prem addendum.
Two, audit log event catalog and a couple sample JSON events, plus export options (S3/EventBridge/HEC pattern).
Three, we schedule an architecture workshop to go through your specific VPC: PrivateLink, egress restrictions, artifact mirroring, and access runbooks.

[26:18] Maya Hernandez: Sounds right.

[26:20] Raj Patel: And key management. We’ll confirm: CMK in our AWS account, rotation policy. HSM optional via CloudHSM behind KMS.

[26:30] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly.

[26:33] Tom Briggs: Also, NDA path for SOC 2 report.

[26:37] Fatima Noor: Yes. We can route you through our evidence process. Typically NDA first, then we share SOC 2 report access. We’ll coordinate with Daniel/Olga on our side, but we’ll keep it simple for you.

[26:53] Maya Hernandez: Great. Can we get the workshop this week.

[26:56] Colin O'Donnell: We’ll propose times after this call.

[27:00] (brief silence)

[27:02] Colin O'Donnell: Any final questions.

[27:05] Raj Patel: Not now. This was good.

[27:07] Elena Smirnova: Thanks.

[27:09] Colin O'Donnell: Thanks all. We’ll follow up by email with the docs and proposed times.

(Transcript continues with light scheduling chatter; recording ends.)
